cues.text: Twelve.
Consolidation.
Let us bring the main ideas of this session together.
First, performance measurement.
Its purpose is to identify whether services are delivering the outcomes that are desired.
It is not enough to run a service; we need to measure it to know whether it achieves what it was meant to achieve.
Closely related to this is benchmarking.
Benchmarking identifies comparative gaps, that is, where our performance differs from that of others or from a chosen standard.
Next, the Balanced Scorecard.
It connects four kinds of measures: financial, customer, process and learning measures.
By linking these together, it gives a rounded view of performance rather than a purely financial one.
Then we turned to resilience.
Resilience engineering designs for failure and adaptation.
In other words, it accepts that failures will occur and builds systems and organisations that can cope with them and adapt.
Within this area, we distinguished two related disciplines.
BCP, or business continuity planning, maintains essential business activities.
DR, or disaster recovery, restores IT.
So BCP is concerned with keeping the business running, while DR is concerned with bringing the technology back.
To decide what comes first, we use BIA, or business impact analysis.
BIA establishes priorities.
Two measures then guide recovery targets.
RTO, the recovery time objective, concerns recovery time, meaning how quickly recovery must happen.
RPO, the recovery point objective, concerns data loss, meaning how much data loss is tolerable.
Finally, the mechanisms that support recovery.
Recovery sites, backups, replication and failover all support recovery.
But having these in place is not enough on its own.
Exercises validate actual capability, showing whether the organisation can truly recover as planned.
